title: Count vowels and consonants in a string (loop through each character, check if a/e/i/o/u).
shortTitle: Count vowels and consonants in a string
keyPoints: Walk the string once, classify each character as a vowel, a consonant, or neither, using two counters.
Lowercase the string first so you only need to test five vowel letters instead of ten.
Use Character.isLetter(c) to skip digits, spaces, and punctuation before classifying.
A clean vowel test is the expression aeiou.indexOf(c) >= 0 which returns true when the character is found.
The algorithm runs in O(n) time and O(1) space because only two integer counters are needed.
The classify-and-tally pattern generalises to counting digits, whitespace, or any character category.

s1_definition.oneliner: Walk the string once, tally vowels and consonants, and skip anything that is not a letter.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Vowel** – one of the five letters a, e, i, o, u (case-insensitive).
- **Consonant** – any letter that is not a vowel.
- **Algorithm** – lowercase the input, loop through each character, check `Character.isLetter(c)` to skip non-letters, then test if the character is a vowel or a consonant and increment the appropriate counter.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time for the single pass and O(1) space for the two counters.
- **Generalisation** – the same classify-and-tally pattern works for counting digits, whitespace, or special characters.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India wants a quick readability metric on Rajesh's chosen account nickname. A clerk reads each letter of the nickname and makes a tally mark in the vowel column for a, e, i, o, u and in the consonant column for every other letter, skipping any numbers or spaces entirely.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Character Classification Flow
  ═════════════════════════════

  Input: "SAV 2001"

  For each character c:
  ┌─────────────────────┐
  │  Is c a letter?     │
  │  isLetter(c)        │
  └─────────┬───────────┘
        yes │         no
            ▼          ▼
  ┌─────────────┐  ┌────────┐
  │ Is vowel?   │  │ SKIP   │
  │ aeiou has c │  │(digit, │
  └──┬──────┬───┘  │space)  │
  yes│      │no    └────────┘
     ▼      ▼
  vowels++ consonants++
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Counting vowels and consonants is a single linear pass with two counters. Lowercase the string first so you only have to test five vowel letters, then loop through each character. For each character, first check whether it is a letter at all, and if it is not a letter, skip it so digits, spaces, and punctuation do not pollute the counts. If it is a letter, test whether it is one of a, e, i, o, u, incrementing the vowel counter if so and the consonant counter otherwise.

In the banking project at National Bank of India, Rajesh used this in an analytics panel that shows how many vowels and consonants a customer's account nickname contains. The `isLetter()` guard is the critical detail, because nicknames frequently contain digits and spaces, and a naive implementation that only checks for vowels and treats everything else as a consonant would wrongly count those non-letters.

The pattern generalises easily to counting digits, whitespace, or any character category by adding more counters and more classification branches. For a functional approach, Java streams with `chars()` and `filter()` offer concise code at the cost of slightly more overhead.

Remember one sentence: lowercase first, guard with `isLetter()`, then classify each character as a vowel or consonant in a single O(n) pass.
